transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-11-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Daniela Cortez (Redwood SE), Ravi Gupta (Aurora Head of ML), Ellen Park (Aurora Infra), Tomás Rivera (Aurora SRE), Priya Menon (Aurora ML)

Summary: quick run through of the reproducible benchmark plan, focused on making the results deterministic and comparable between Redwood hosted, Redwood private (VPC) and Aurora on-prem lab.

Topics covered: load replay methodology, prompt set selection, KV-cache warmup, batching policies, quantization flip tests, network egress and VPC peering implications.

Action items (captured during call): see metadata list.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. we've got about an hour and a bit; main goal is to land on a reproducible benchmark plan that you can run in your lab and compare to our hosted numbers. hi ravi, tomás, ellen, priya.
[00:18] Ravi (Aurora): thanks, yeah excited — we want a like-for-like set so our infra folks can justify either dedicated or hosting. main concerns are latency tails and of course cost.
[00:33] Marcus (Redwood SE): great, so i'll walk through the harness architecture first, then we can map it to your network topology. important note: we emphasize trace-driven load replay not synthetic steady-state traffic. that way you capture realistic seq len, prompt mix, and arrival patterns.
[00:49] Tomás (Aurora SRE): when you say trace-driven, do you mean you want us to export live production traces? we have PII redaction concerns.
[00:58] Daniela (Redwood): good q. we prefer anonymized traces with token-level timing only — token counts and inter-arrival times. remove user ids and payloads. we provide a small script to strip PII in the harness.
[01:14] Ellen (Aurora Infra): also curious about KV cache warmup. in on-prem tests we saw weird variance when the cache wasn't warmed properly. what's your recommended warmup protocol?
[01:26] Marcus: yep, KV-cash — sorry, KV cache — warmup is critical. our recommended protocol is staged warmup: first run a warmup pass using the top-10% most common prompt prefixes for 10k tokens, then run a prioritized cache fill where the harness replays high-frequency user flows for 15 minutes. include a cool-down to emulate cache eviction patterns for long-tail tests.
[01:49] Ravi: can you quantify the difference? like what do we expect for p95 vs cold?
[01:56] Marcus: on similar models we've seen p95 improve from ~220ms cold to ~95ms after steady-state KV warmup with batching tuned. but quantization changes that; we'll get to that. numbers will vary with sequence length and batch sizing.
[02:11] Sofia: quick interjection — on the subject of like-for-like comparisons, we avoid vendor nomenclature causing unfair comparisons. we provide a config file that pins model version, tokenizer, and deterministic sampling seeds. that prevents accidental quality differences.
[02:29] Priya (Aurora ML): about prompts — do you have an example set? our use-case is retrieval-augmented generation + short completion (~60 tokens).
[02:36] Marcus: yes we ship three canonical prompt sets: short-complete, mid-dialogue, and long-context summarization. we'll ask you to pick the closest match and also provide a 1k-sample distribution for token lengths.
[02:50] Priya: ok we'll extract that.
[02:55] Tomás: network — when you run private deployment tests, how do you account for egress latency if we peer VPC to Redwood? our on-prem path goes through an edge proxy.
[03:05] Daniela: capture the full network RTT in your trace. for fair comparisons we recommend recording both client-to-edge and edge-to-hosted hops, then run tests with and without peered routes. that surfaces any additional serialization or TLS costs.
[03:22] Ellen: for on-prem, we have jumbo frame settings and some custom NIC offloads; could that skew results?
[03:28] Marcus: yes hardware tuning can skew headroom. in the runbook we include an "infrastructure baseline" checklist: NIC offload settings, kernel network tuning, cpu governor, and isol cpus for the infer nodes. if you deviate, annotate the run result so we can correlate.
[03:47] Ravi: another question: quantization — when we go from fp16 to 4-bit q, how do you measure quality regressions? automated evals or manual checks?
[03:57] Sofia: both. we have an eval harness that runs a gold set of scoring prompts and computes BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics plus embedding-sim for semantic similarity. we also ask for a small human review sample for any regression flagged above a threshold. that way we capture both numeric and subjective differences.
[04:15] Marcus: add to that — include gen-seed so sampling is fixed. that ensures we compare like-for-like rather than sample noise.
[04:24] Priya: how do you recommend running quantization flip tests? run the same workload with fp16, int8, and q4a?
[04:31] Marcus: yes run a flip matrix. baseline fp16, then q8 (if available), q4 standard, and q4+ (if you want to push smaller kernels). log per-token latency, p50/p95/p99, and the eval score. we also capture throughput at varying concurrency points.
[04:47] Tomás: is there an automated script to swap the model variant and re-run? we prefer not to rebuild containers each time.
[04:52] Marcus: the harness supports hot-swap calls to the runtime with model variant tags; on Redwood Private the control-plane can pin model variants without redeploy. on your on-prem you'll need the new quantized artifact, but the harness automates model load and warmup via API calls.
[05:08] Ravi: you mentioned batching — how do you select batch sizes for latency-sensitive workloads?
[05:14] Daniela: we recommend profiling with a binary search approach: start with min batch of 1 and increase exponentially until you hit SLO breach on p95. the harness will do that automatically in an "auto-batch sweep" mode and output recommended batch size and suggested concurrency.
[05:28] Ellen: what about GPU memory constraints with bigger batches + kv cache? on our A100s we can run into OOM for long contexts.
[05:36] Marcus: yep, the runbook includes a memory model estimator: given model size, seq len, kv cache length, and quantization footprint, it predicts peak GPU mem. we also log allocator metrics during runs so you can correlate OOMs.
[05:50] Speaker 2: (inaudible) so is there a standard csv of metrics?
[05:54] Sofia: yes, we standardize on a CSV with these columns: run_id, model_tag, quantization, batch_size, concurrency, seq_len_avg, tokens_generated, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, throughput_tps, gesture_cost_estimate, env_notes. plus a JSON trace artifact with per-request timings.
[06:12] Ravi: cost estimate is important; can you surface token-cost per 1M tokens?
[06:15] Marcus: we'll include cost-per-token estimates for hosted and a per-hour GPU cost for private, normalized to the same token mix. this is heuristic but good for decisioning.
[06:25] Priya: are there any pitfalls you often see running these like-for-like tests?
[06:29] Daniela: common pitfalls: mismatch in tokenizer versions, different random seeds, not warming the kv cache, and network egress asymmetry. sometimes infra teams inadvertently attach a debugging profiler which adds latency. note those in env_notes.
[06:44] Tomás: about reproducibility: if we run the harness twice on the same config, what variance do you expect?
[06:50] Marcus: under controlled infra and with cache warm, typical variance for p95 is within 5-8% across runs. if you see more, that's a signal to look at network jitter or CPU stealing.
[07:03] Ravi: ok, let's talk timeline and file sharing.
[07:06] Sofia: we'll share three artifacts after this call: 1) the benchmark harness repo + quickstart, 2) a runbook with the infrastructure checklist and warmup protocol, 3) canonical prompt sets and eval goldset. link will be posted in the CRM and in the shared drive.
[07:22] Ellen: please include an example results workbook so our PMs can see the cc summary.
[07:28] Sofia: yes, sample workbook included.
[07:31] Priya: for the goldset, we have some privacy-sensitive items. can you host a scoring endpoint so we can submit hashed prompts and get metrics back?
[07:40] Daniela: we can support a blinded scoring endpoint for hosted customers. for private/on-prem we provide the scoring harness you run locally and then upload aggregate metrics only.
[07:52] Tomás: last question — on-prem network peering: if we peer into Redwood, do you accept a direct VPC peering or do you require a VPN?
[07:59] Sofia: we support both. for regulated customers we recommend private peering with strict ACLs and use of customer-managed KMS for keys. we'll include network examples in the runbook.
[08:12] Sofia: ok wrapping up — recap of next steps: Marcus will push repo, Ravi team will extract prompt set and schedule two replay runs (small/large), Tomás will export network egress paths and firewall rules. Redwood will host a follow-up network deep-dive.
[08:27] Ravi: thanks, appreciate the level of detail.
[08:30] Sofia: thanks all — we'll follow up in CRM and send calendar invite for the deep-dive. bye.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

Notes: occasional transcription errors present (e.g., "KV-cash"), speaker labels may be fuzzy in sections. Links referenced (will be shared): https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-bench-harness (repo), https://drive.redwood.ai/shared/aurora-bench-results (shared folder).
